one_liner: Distributed pandas/NumPy-API engine built on Mars. On 100 GB-1 TB TPC-H it beats Dask DataFrame, Modin and pandas-on-Spark.
what_it_does: Xorbits scales pandas and NumPy code across the cores of one machine or across a cluster. You change `import pandas as pd` to `import xorbits.pandas as pd` (the same works for numpy, and there are thin sklearn, XGBoost, LightGBM and HuggingFace datasets wrappers). Execution is deferred: it builds a plan and runs it on repr/str, on output methods such as to_csv, when metadata is missing, or when you call xorbits.run(). Unlike Dask, you never set partitions or chunk sizes or call repartition/compute. Chunking happens automatically.
how_it_is_fast: Data is split into chunks that plain pandas/NumPy runs in separate worker processes, so there is no GIL, and intermediate results go to a shared-memory storage service (disk, mmap or Vineyard backends are optional). The core idea is dynamic (iterative) tiling: Xorbits executes the first chunks, collects their real shapes, sizes and dtypes, and only then tiles the rest of the graph. That lets it choose tree-reduce or shuffle-reduce for groupby.agg, merge small chunks up to chunk_store_limit (512 MB by default), and handle skewed joins that Dask and Modin partition blindly. It adds coloring-based graph-level fusion of the chunk graph into subtasks, operator fusion through NumExpr/JAX/CuPy, column pruning, and breadth-first plus locality-aware scheduling onto NUMA-node or GPU 'bands'. The paper's ablation credits dynamic tiling with 7.08x (TPC-H Q2, SF1000) and 10.59x (Q7, SF100), and graph fusion with 3.80x (Q7) and 2.04x (Q8).
when_to_use: Existing pandas code on 100 GB-1 TB Parquet/CSV that no longer fits one node, when you want to keep the pandas API rather than rewrite into Spark SQL or Dask idioms.
Merges between a huge fact table and a tiny dimension table (skewed keys). There Dask and Modin stall on one core; the paper measured 29x and 37x on TPCx-AI UC10 (34 GB joined to 3.2 MB).
Single-node multi-core speedup on 20 GB-class CSV feature-engineering pipelines. The paper reports 2.65x over Modin on census and 3.86x over PySpark on plasticc, with single-threaded pandas slowest.
Mixed dataframe and distributed-array work (QR, linear regression) where you would otherwise pair Dask DataFrame with Dask Array. The paper reports 5.88x and 1.74x average throughput over Dask Array.
Teams already running Kubernetes, SLURM or a plain supervisor/worker cluster (the xorbits-supervisor and xorbits-worker CLIs) that want a pandas-shaped front end.
when_not_to_use: Data that fits comfortably in one machine's RAM when raw speed is the goal. The paper compares only against pandas-API frameworks, never DuckDB, Polars or SQL engines, and it calls pandas-API TPC-H 'fundamentally unfair' against SQL systems.
Small or interactive workloads. Startup is slow (the docs say to call xorbits.init() before timing), and too many chunks make the supervisor spend its time scheduling.

Anything that needs an actively maintained dependency. The last release was 0.8.2 (2024-12-26) and the last main commit 2025-04-21. There are 84 open issues, including open correctness bugs (#691 reset_index on unexecuted groupby output, #671 head(100) wrong on TPC-H Q18 output).
Python 3.13+: PyPI has wheels only for CPython 3.9-3.12.

GPU (cuDF/CuPy) production use. Many GPU-labelled bugs are still open, such as nunique failing on GPU (#344), cuDF NA deserialization errors (#406) and CUDA memory not being released on shutdown (#377).

integration.dependencies: xoscar (actor runtime), numpy, pandas, scipy, scikit-learn, pyarrow, fsspec, cloudpickle, pyyaml, psutil, tornado, sqlalchemy, defusedxml, tqdm, uvloop (non-Windows). Optional: ray, kubernetes, vineyard, jax, numexpr/lz4, s3fs, adlfs, datasets.
integration.min_toolchain: Python >=3.9. PyPI 0.8.2 wheels cover CPython 3.9-3.12, and building from source needs Cython >=0.29.33. setup.cfg declares pandas >=1.0, but CI carries a TODO that pandas 2.2.3 does not work well with numpy 2.2 / pyarrow 19.
integration.platforms: Wheels for Linux x86-64/aarch64 (manylinux2014), macOS x86-64/arm64 and Windows amd64. Cluster deployment is via CLI, Kubernetes (including EKS) or SLURM. Optional NVIDIA GPU through cuDF/CuPy (gpu=True on loaders).
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. Execution runs in separate worker processes behind a client session created by xorbits.init() (or implicitly on the first compute).
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — it is not API-compatible with Dask. Code written with dd.*, .compute(), map_partitions or repartition must be rewritten as plain pandas-style code (the Xorbits equivalent of map_partitions is map_chunk). As a pandas replacement it is close to drop-in: the paper reports 96.7% coverage on 30 pandas asv cases, against 46.7% for Dask. Unimplemented methods fall back to pandas (see gotchas).

gotchas: Silent-scale fallback: any pandas method Xorbits has not implemented is emitted as a RuntimeWarning '<Type>.<method> will fallback to Pandas'. It then runs after rechunking the whole object into one chunk (core/adapter.py), so a single worker must hold the full frame. On 1 TB data that means OOM.

Deferred execution plus iterative tiling means a statement can trigger partial execution mid-plan whenever metadata such as a post-filter shape is unknown. Errors and cost appear later than they would in pandas. Call xorbits.run() to force evaluation, and warm up with xorbits.init() before benchmarking.
Performance depends on chunk_store_limit (512 MB by default). The docs say raising it helps little on CPU but should be raised on GPU. chunk_size= on constructors is meant for debugging.
Open operational bugs include 'Too many open files' (#769, #731), gzip read_csv using only one core (#738), and read_parquet memory-allocation errors (#729).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over Modin when data exceeds one node or merges are skewed: in the paper Modin on Ray OOMed on SF1000 and was 37x slower on skewed UC10, even though both reach 96.7% pandas-API coverage. FireDucks and cuDF (cudf.pandas) are single-machine pandas accelerators with much larger speedups over pandas, so Xorbits is only the right choice when you need multi-node scale-out behind the pandas API.
verified_claims_summary: The ICDE 2024 paper is by the Xorbits authors. Setup: AWS r6i workers, each r6i.8xlarge with 32 vCPU and 256 GB, CPU model unnamed; 4 workers for TPC-H SF100 (36 GB Parquet) and 16 for SF1000 (358 GB). Versions were Xorbits 0.6.3, Dask 2023.9, Modin 0.24.1 on Ray, pandas-on-Spark 3.5.0 and pandas 2.1.1, all with default configs, averaged over 7 runs with the max and min dropped. Xorbits averaged 2.66x over the fastest baseline on operations every system supports and was 29x/37x faster than Dask/Modin on skewed TPCx-AI UC10. TPC-H relative times count only the queries each baseline finished. The docs' '~8x DaskDF, ~4x Modin at SF100' figure gives no hardware.
status_note: Stale: last release 0.8.2 in December 2024, last main commit April 2025 (cuDF 25.2 compat), later pushes are dependabot branches only. It is Apache-2.0 and pip-installable with prebuilt wheels, but the large Mars-derived codebase is not something you can realistically vendor or maintain yourself.
